proof_summary: For an odd prime divisor \(p\mid n\), multiplicative-order factors \(2^{jd}-1\) and factorial valuation bounds show that if \(n=pt\) with \(t\ge2\), then \(p\mid a(n-1)\), forcing the impossible conclusion \(p\mid2\); hence a composite candidate could only be \(2^v\), but the exact calculation \(v_2(a(2^v-1))=v-1\) rules this out. Once \(n\) is prime, if the order \(d\) of \(2\bmod n\) were less than \(n-1\), the factor \(2^d-1\) in the defining product would force \(n\) to divide its numerator, contradicting the original divisibility together with \(n\nmid a(n-1)\); thus \(d=n-1\).
